title: Why Do Soda Bubbles Rise From the Same Spots? #science
description:
Each string of bubbles in a glass of soda usually starts at a tiny hollow fibre, like lint from a towel, stuck to the glass. A brand-new bubble is so small that surface tension squeezes its gas back into the drink, so bubbles need a pocket of gas that is already there. The fibre traps one, fills with carbon dioxide from the drink, and releases a bubble again and again. (Most of this research was done on champagne; the same physics applies to soda.)

More on everyday molecules: Why microwaves don't heat food from the inside https://youtu.be/ri17BZl0Iq8

Sources
- Liger-Belair, G. et al. (2002), Kinetics of gas discharging in a glass of champagne: the role of nucleation sites, Langmuir 18: 1294–1301
- Liger-Belair, G. (2003), The Physics and Chemistry of Champagne, Scientific American 288(1): 80–85
- Liger-Belair, G. (2005), The physics and chemistry behind the bubbling properties of champagne and sparkling wines, J. Agric. Food Chem. 53: 2788–2802
- Jones, S. F., Evans, G. M. & Galvin, K. P. (1999), Bubble nucleation from gas cavities — a review, Adv. Colloid Interface Sci. 80: 27–50

Next time, look for the starting point of each bubble string. How many can you count?

subtitles: Why do soda bubbles rise from the same spots?
Each string usually starts at a tiny speck of lint stuck to the glass.
Soda is packed with carbon dioxide, forced in under pressure.
Open it, and the gas wants out, but starting a bubble is hard.
A brand-new bubble is so tiny that surface tension squeezes its gas back into the drink.
It needs a head start: a pocket of gas that's already there.
Hollow fibres, like towel lint, trap exactly that.
Each one fills with gas and lets go of a bubble, again and again.
The gas comes from the drink.
The starting points are bits of lint on the glass.
